lessons.title: Print the sequence
lessons.intro: Your sample S07 is ready: ATGCGC. Please check it before we run the full batch.
lessons.doneSub: Your report matches the facility read, letter for letter.

questions.ask: What does R print for the sample?
questions.hint: Quote marks make text. A name without quotes means the value stored in it.
questions.ok: sample without quotes is the stored value; "sample" in quotes is the word itself.

fb.b: In quotes, "sample" is a word, not the variable.
fb.c: R keeps the quote marks when it prints text.

questions.bridge: count the bases in the sample.
questions.label: The facility read for sample S07: ATGCGC.

science.title: Why check the read first?
science.text: A swapped tube or file is the most common reason a whole batch of results is wrong. Printing the sample first is the cheapest check there is.

codeNote.title: Text and names
codeNote.text: `x = "AT"` stores text in `x`. `print(x)` shows the stored value; `print("x")` shows the word x itself. R prints text with its quote marks.

questions.ask: Count the bases in the sample
questions.hint: One function counts the characters inside a piece of text.
questions.ok: nchar() counts the characters in the text: 6 bases.

fb.b: length(sample) is 1: one piece of text.
fb.c: sum() cannot add text, so R stops with an error.
fb.d: print() shows the text; it does not count it.

questions.bridge: add the sample ID to make a label.
questions.label: The six bases of the sample, with their count still unknown.

science.title: Why count the bases?
science.text: The facility reports read length for every sample. If your count differs from theirs, the file you have is not the read they sequenced.

codeNote.title: Counting with `nchar()` and `length()`
codeNote.text: `nchar("cell")` counts the characters in a piece of text: 4. `length(x)` counts items in a vector, so `length("cell")` is 1.

questions.ask: Make a label from the ID and the sample
questions.hint: paste() puts something between its pieces by default.
questions.ok: paste() joins its pieces with a space by default: "S07 ATGCGC".

fb.b: That is what paste0() gives, with no space.
fb.c: Without quotes, id and sample mean their stored values.

questions.bridge: the facility's template script stops with an error.
questions.label: The ID S07 and the sample ATGCGC, about to be joined into one label.

science.title: Why label every read?
science.text: Facilities run hundreds of samples at once. An ID next to every read means a result can always be traced back to its tube.

codeNote.title: Joining text with `paste()`
codeNote.text: `paste("a", "b")` joins its pieces with a space: "a b". `paste0("a", "b")` joins with nothing between: "ab".

questions.ask: The facility's template stops. Which line?
questions.hint: Compare the capital letters with the names you made.
questions.ok: R is case-sensitive: Sample and sample are different names, and only sample exists.

fb.c: print() is fine; R never reaches it.

questions.bridge: the facility sends a lowercase copy to match.
questions.label: The facility's label template stops with: object 'Sample' not found.

science.title: Why a single letter matters
science.text: A script that stops halfway can leave a results file half written. Catching the error early keeps a broken report from reaching the facility.

codeNote.title: Names are case-sensitive
codeNote.text: R treats `Count`, `count` and `COUNT` as three different names. Using a name that was never created stops R with "object not found".

pics.text: Please use our label template for every sample.

questions.ask: Match the facility's lowercase copy
questions.hint: Capital and small letters count as different in R.
questions.ok: toupper() turns "atgcgc" into "ATGCGC", which equals sample.

fb.b: tolower() keeps it lowercase, so it does not equal "ATGCGC": FALSE.
fb.c: nchar() gives 6, and 6 does not equal "ATGCGC": FALSE.
fb.d: paste() keeps the lowercase text: FALSE.

questions.label: The facility copy in lowercase, atgcgc, next to your sample ATGCGC.

science.title: Why lowercase copies happen
science.text: Some tools write bases in lowercase, for example to mark low-quality or masked regions. Matching the case first avoids false mismatches.

codeNote.title: Changing case
codeNote.text: `toupper("ab")` gives "AB" and `tolower("AB")` gives "ab". `==` compares two values and gives `TRUE` or `FALSE`; text must match letter for letter.

lessons.title: GC content
lessons.intro: My notebook says this sample is 35.3% GC. Can you check it in R?
lessons.doneSub: 66.7%, not 35.3%: the order of operations made the difference.

questions.ask: What does R print?
questions.hint: Which happens first in maths: + or /?
questions.ok: R divides before it adds: 2 + 2/6 = 2.333333.

fb.b: That needs brackets: (2 + 2) / 6.
fb.c: That ignores the division by 6.

questions.bridge: add brackets so the sum happens first.
questions.label: Sample ATGCGC with its 2 G and 2 C bases highlighted.

science.title: What GC content is
science.text: GC content is the share of a sequence that is G or C. G-C pairs hold three hydrogen bonds instead of two, so GC-rich DNA melts at a higher temperature.

codeNote.title: Order of operations
codeNote.text: R follows maths order: `^` first, then `*` and `/`, then `+` and `-`. Brackets go first of all: `(1 + 2) * 3` is 9, but `1 + 2 * 3` is 7.

questions.ask: Add brackets so the sum happens first
questions.hint: GC content is a share of the whole length.
questions.ok: (2 + 2) / 6 = 0.6666667: the brackets make the sum happen first.

fb.b: That multiplies: 24.
fb.c: That subtracts: -2.
fb.d: That raises 4 to the 6th power: 4096.

questions.bridge: turn the fraction into a percentage.
questions.label: 4 G or C bases out of 6; the operator is the blank.

science.title: Why a fraction first?
science.text: A fraction from 0 to 1 compares directly between sequences of different lengths. Percentages are for reports; fractions are for calculations.

codeNote.title: Brackets
codeNote.text: Anything inside `( )` is worked out first. `(a + b) / n` adds, then divides; `a + b / n` divides `b` only.

questions.ask: Turn the fraction into a percentage
questions.hint: The second number in round() is how many decimals to keep.
questions.ok: gc * 100 is 66.66667, and round(..., 1) keeps one decimal: 66.7.

fb.b: That is before rounding.
fb.c: That would be round(..., 0).

questions.label: A GC gauge waiting for the percentage.

science.title: How precise to report
science.text: GC content is usually reported to one decimal place. More digits than your measurement supports suggests precision you do not have.

codeNote.title: Rounding with `round()`
codeNote.text: `round(x, d)` keeps `d` decimal places: `round(3.14159, 2)` is 3.14 and `round(3.14159)` is 3.

questions.ask: Partner's notebook says 35.3%. Which line?
questions.hint: Which line mixes + with / and * without brackets?
questions.ok: Without brackets, only c_count is divided and multiplied: 2 + 33.33 = 35.3.

fb.b: Storing 2 is fine.
fb.d: Rounding is fine; the value is already wrong.

questions.bridge: write the line for the lab report.
questions.label: Your lab partner's notebook says 35.3%; yours says 66.7%.

science.title: Why two notebooks disagree
science.text: When two people get different numbers from one sample, check the calculation before rerunning the experiment. It is cheaper and usually the cause.

codeNote.title: Reading a long formula
codeNote.text: In `a + b / c * d`, R works out `b / c * d` first, from left to right, then adds `a`. Brackets around `(a + b)` change which numbers are divided.

pics.text: My notebook says 35.3%. Which of us is right?

questions.ask: Build the line for the lab report
questions.hint: Wrap paste(...) inside print(...).
questions.ok: paste() joins the three pieces with spaces: "GC: 66.7 %".
questions.label: A blank line in the lab report, waiting for the GC content.

science.title: Why print a full line?
science.text: A labelled line like "GC: 66.7 %" can go straight into a report or a log, so nobody has to remember which number was which.

codeNote.title: Nesting functions
codeNote.text: `print(paste("a", "b"))` runs the inner function first, then hands its result to the outer one. Every `(` needs its own `)`.

questions.wrongBuild: The line is print(paste("GC:", pct, "%")): paste() joins its pieces with spaces.

lessons.title: Count the AT bases
lessons.intro: Can someone check this 10-base read with me? I keep getting odd numbers.
lessons.doneSub: 3 codons, 1 leftover base, 50% AT, and an ATG start.

questions.ask: How many full codons are in the read?
questions.hint: %/% is whole-number division.
questions.ok: 10 bases hold 3 full codons: %/% divides and drops the remainder.

fb.b: That is n / 3, which keeps the fraction.
fb.c: That is the remainder, n %% 3.

questions.label: A 10-base read split into groups of three.

science.title: Codons
science.text: The genetic code is read three bases at a time; each triplet is a codon. Counting full codons tells you how many amino acids the read could encode.

codeNote.title: Whole-number division
codeNote.text: `7 %/% 2` is 3: how many whole 2s fit in 7. `7 %% 2` is 1: what is left over. `7 / 2` is 3.5.

questions.ask: Find the leftover bases
questions.hint: Which operator gives the remainder?
questions.ok: 10 %% 3 is 1: one base left after 3 full codons.

fb.b: That gives 3, the number of full codons.
fb.c: That gives 3.333333.
fb.d: That gives 7.

questions.label: Three full codons and one base left over at the end.

science.title: Why the leftover matters
science.text: A read whose length is not a multiple of 3 cannot be translated cleanly from its first base. The leftover often means the read was cut mid-codon.

codeNote.title: Remainders with `%%`
codeNote.text: `x %% y` is what is left after dividing `x` by `y` as many whole times as possible: `10 %% 4` is 2, and `9 %% 3` is 0.

questions.ask: What share of the read is A or T?
questions.hint: Brackets first, then / and * from left to right.
questions.ok: (10 - 5) / 10 * 100 = 50: half the bases are A or T.

fb.b: That is n - gc, the count, not the share.
fb.c: That is the fraction before * 100.

questions.bridge: a classmate asks why their AT count is -5.
questions.label: The read with its A and T bases highlighted.

science.title: Why AT and GC add up
science.text: Every base is A, T, G or C, so the AT share is everything that is not GC. Checking that the two add to 100% catches miscounts.

codeNote.title: Formulas with several steps
codeNote.text: R works through `(n - gc) / n * 100` in order: the bracket first, then `/` and `*` from left to right.

questions.ask: A classmate gets -5 AT bases. Which line?
questions.hint: Which subtraction runs the wrong way round?
questions.ok: gc - n subtracts the wrong way round: 5 - 10 = -5. It should be n - gc.

fb.b: There are 5 G or C bases.
fb.d: print() shows what at holds.

questions.label: A classmate on the forum gets -5 AT bases from the same read.

science.title: Sanity checks
science.text: A count of bases can never be negative. Checking that a result is possible at all catches many mistakes before anyone reads the number.

codeNote.title: Subtraction order
codeNote.text: `a - b` and `b - a` give the same size with opposite signs: `10 - 4` is 6, `4 - 10` is -6.

pics.text: Why does my code say I have -5 AT bases?

questions.ask: Print the first codon of the read
questions.hint: substr(text, start, stop)
questions.ok: substr(read, 1, 3) takes characters 1 to 3: "ATG", the start codon.
questions.label: The first three bases of the read, about to be cut out.

science.title: ATG, the start codon
science.text: Translation almost always begins at ATG, which codes for methionine. Finding it at the start suggests the read begins at a gene.

codeNote.title: Cutting text with `substr()`
codeNote.text: `substr(text, start, stop)` returns the characters from position `start` to `stop`. `substr("biology", 1, 3)` is "bio".

questions.wrongBuild: The line is print(substr(read, 1, 3)): substr() takes the characters from the first position to the second.

lessons.title: Both strands
lessons.intro: Your poster shows both DNA strands. I will check the pairing before the session.
lessons.doneSub: Both strands pair correctly, and the poster label is ready.

questions.ask: What is the second strand?
questions.hint: Each letter in the first set becomes the letter in the same place in the second.
questions.ok: chartr() swaps each letter: A to T, T to A, G to C, C to G.

fb.b: That is the original strand: chartr() changes every letter.
fb.c: That is the complement written backwards.

questions.bridge: check both strands are the same length.
questions.label: The top strand ATGCGC, with the bottom strand still to fill in.

science.title: Base pairing
science.text: A always pairs with T, and G with C. So one strand fully determines the other, which is how cells copy DNA.

codeNote.title: Swapping letters with `chartr()`
codeNote.text: `chartr(old, new, text)` replaces each letter of `old` with the letter in the same position of `new`: `chartr("ab", "xy", "abba")` is "xyyx".

questions.ask: Check both strands are the same length
questions.hint: Which operator asks "is equal to"?
questions.ok: Both strands have 6 bases, so == gives TRUE.

fb.b: A single = names or stores; here R stops with an error.
fb.c: != asks "not equal", which is FALSE.
fb.d: 6 < 6 is FALSE.

questions.bridge: join the strands for the poster.
questions.label: Top and bottom strands, 6 bases each.

science.title: Why check lengths?
science.text: Every base pairs with exactly one partner, so the two strands must be the same length. A mismatch means a base was dropped.

codeNote.title: Comparing values
codeNote.text: `==` asks whether two values are equal, `!=` whether they differ, and `<`, `>` compare size. A single `=` stores a value instead.

questions.ask: Join the strands for the poster
questions.hint: sep sets what goes between the pieces.
questions.ok: sep = "/" puts a slash between the pieces instead of a space.

fb.b: That is the default separator, a space.
fb.c: paste() returns one piece of text, not two.

questions.bridge: a reviewer comments on your poster.
questions.label: Both strands, about to be joined with a slash.

science.title: Writing both strands
science.text: Posters and papers often show a duplex as top/bottom strands so readers can check the pairing by eye.

codeNote.title: The `sep` argument
codeNote.text: `paste("a", "b", sep = "-")` gives "a-b". `sep` sets what goes between the pieces; the default is a single space.

questions.ask: The reviewer flags the pairing. Which line?
questions.hint: Check which letter each old letter turns into.
questions.ok: new lists the letters in the wrong order: A stays A and T stays T. It should be "TACG".

fb.a: old lists the four bases in order.
fb.c: chartr() is used correctly; new is wrong.
fb.d: print() shows what comp holds.

questions.bridge: add a label for the poster.
questions.label: The poster reviewer says the second strand pairs A with A.

science.title: Why reviewers check pairing
science.text: A wrong complement makes every later step wrong: primers, probes and alignments all rely on the second strand.

codeNote.title: Checking a letter map
codeNote.text: In `chartr("ATGC", new, x)`, the first letter of `new` replaces A, the second replaces T, and so on. Read the two sets in pairs to check them.

pics.text: Your second strand pairs A with A. Is the complement right?

questions.ask: Add the sample ID to the poster label
questions.hint: One version of paste adds no space.
questions.ok: paste0() joins with nothing in between: "S07_ATGCGC/TACGCG".

fb.b: paste() adds a space: "S07_ ATGCGC/TACGCG".
fb.c: nchar() counts one piece of text; with two, R stops with an error.
fb.d: toupper() takes one piece of text, so R stops with an error.

questions.label: The poster label: the ID S07_ followed by the pair.

science.title: Labels on posters
science.text: Joining the sample ID to the sequence on one line means a figure can be matched to its tube even after it is printed.

codeNote.title: `paste()` and `paste0()`
codeNote.text: `paste0("a", "b")` gives "ab"; `paste("a", "b")` gives "a b". Use `paste0()` when the separator is already part of the text.

lessons.title: Store the scores
lessons.intro: Quality scores are exported one per base. Position 0 is the first base.
lessons.doneSub: Three of four bases pass Q30, and R counts from 1, not 0.

questions.ask: What is the score of the second base?
questions.hint: Where does R start counting positions?
questions.ok: R counts positions from 1, so scores[2] is the second score, 36.

fb.b: That is scores[1]: R starts at 1.
fb.c: That is the third score; R does not start counting at 0.

questions.bridge: pick the last score without counting.
questions.label: Quality scores for the four bases of a read; the second is unknown.

science.title: Quality scores
science.text: A Phred quality score of 30 means a 1 in 1,000 chance the base call is wrong; 20 means 1 in 100. Higher is better.

codeNote.title: Vectors and positions
codeNote.text: `c(4, 8, 15)` makes a vector of three numbers. `v[1]` is the first item and `v[3]` the third: positions in R start at 1.

questions.ask: Pick the last score without counting
questions.hint: The last position is the same as the number of items.
questions.ok: length(scores) is 4, so scores[4] is the last score, 12.

fb.b: nchar() counts digits, so scores[c(2, 2, 2, 2)] prints 36 four times.
fb.c: sum is 116, and there is no 116th score: NA.
fb.d: max is 38, and there is no 38th score: NA.

questions.label: The same four scores; the last one is unknown.

science.title: Why the last bases matter
science.text: Quality usually drops towards the end of a read. The last score is a quick check of how far the read can be trusted.

codeNote.title: Counting items with `length()`
codeNote.text: `length(v)` gives the number of items in `v`, so `v[length(v)]` is always the last item, however long `v` is.

questions.ask: Which bases pass Q30?
questions.hint: A comparison on a vector checks every item.
questions.ok: The comparison runs on every score at once, giving one TRUE or FALSE each.

fb.b: Comparisons on a vector give one answer per item.
fb.c: That is the scores themselves, not the comparison.

questions.bridge: the manual's position 0 trips up a script.
questions.label: The four scores against a cutoff line at 30.

science.title: The Q30 cutoff
science.text: Many labs keep bases at Q30 or above, about 99.9% accurate. Bases below it are trimmed before analysis.

codeNote.title: Comparing a whole vector
codeNote.text: `v > 5` compares every item of `v` with 5 and returns one `TRUE` or `FALSE` per item: `c(3, 8) > 5` is FALSE TRUE.

questions.ask: The manual's numbering breaks a script. Which line?
questions.hint: Which line uses the manual's numbering?
questions.ok: R positions start at 1. scores[0] selects nothing, so R prints numeric(0).

fb.c: print() shows what first holds: nothing.

questions.label: A script written from the manual prints numeric(0) instead of the first score.

science.title: Reading manuals critically
science.text: Instrument software is often written in languages that count from 0. When you move numbers into R, check which counting the documentation uses.

codeNote.title: Position 0 in R
codeNote.text: Some languages count from 0, but R counts from 1. `v[0]` returns an empty vector, which R prints as `numeric(0)`, without an error.

questions.ask: Keep only the bases that pass
questions.hint: Put the comparison inside the square brackets.
questions.ok: scores[scores >= 30] keeps only the items where the comparison is TRUE.
questions.label: The four scores; the one below 30 is about to be dropped.

science.title: Trimming low-quality bases
science.text: Dropping bases below a cutoff before alignment reduces false variant calls caused by sequencing errors.

codeNote.title: Filtering with `[ ]`
codeNote.text: Putting a `TRUE`/`FALSE` vector inside `[ ]` keeps the items marked `TRUE`: `c(4, 9)[c(FALSE, TRUE)]` is 9.

questions.wrongBuild: The line is good = scores[scores >= 30]: a TRUE/FALSE vector inside [ ] keeps the TRUE items.

lessons.title: Average with mean()
lessons.intro: My spreadsheet average for this read is 23.2. Does R agree?
lessons.doneSub: Mean 29, median 33, and the gap handled honestly.

questions.ask: What is the mean quality of the read?
questions.hint: mean = total divided by count.
questions.ok: mean() adds the scores (116) and divides by how many there are (4): 29.

fb.b: That is the sum.
fb.c: That is the number of scores.

questions.label: Four quality scores with their average still unknown.

science.title: Mean read quality
science.text: The mean quality summarises a whole read in one number, so reads can be ranked or filtered quickly.

codeNote.title: Averages with `mean()`
codeNote.text: `mean(v)` adds the items of `v` and divides by how many there are: `mean(c(2, 4, 9))` is 5.

questions.ask: Find the middle score instead
questions.hint: Which average is the middle value?
questions.ok: median() sorts the scores (12 30 36 38) and averages the middle two: 33.

fb.b: mean() gives 29.
fb.c: max() gives 38.
fb.d: sum() gives 116.

questions.label: The scores sorted from lowest to highest; the middle value is unknown.

science.title: Mean or median?
science.text: One low score, like 12, pulls the mean down but barely moves the median. Comparing the two shows whether a few bad bases skew the average.

codeNote.title: The middle value with `median()`
codeNote.text: `median(v)` sorts `v` and takes the middle item, or the average of the two middle items when there is an even number.

questions.ask: One score is missing. What is the mean now?
questions.hint: What can R say about an average with a missing number?
questions.ok: Any NA makes mean() return NA, because the missing value could be anything.

fb.b: That is the mean of the other three; R does not skip NA unless told to.
fb.c: NA is not treated as zero.

questions.bridge: tell mean() to skip the gap.
questions.label: The read again, with the third score missing.

science.title: Why scores go missing
science.text: Instruments write NA when a base could not be called, for example in a bubble or a dim cluster. The read is not empty; one value is unknown.

codeNote.title: Missing values: `NA`
codeNote.text: `NA` marks a missing value. Most calculations that touch an `NA` return `NA`, so one gap can turn a whole summary into `NA`.

questions.ask: Skip the missing score
questions.hint: You want to remove the NA.
questions.ok: na.rm = TRUE removes the NA first, then averages 38, 36 and 12.

fb.b: FALSE keeps the NA, so the answer stays NA.
fb.c: na.rm needs TRUE or FALSE; NA stops R with an error.
fb.d: 0 counts as FALSE, so the answer stays NA.

questions.label: The three known scores, with the gap set aside.

science.title: Removing NA honestly
science.text: Skipping missing values is fine for a summary, but say how many were skipped, so a reader knows the average rests on fewer bases.

codeNote.title: Optional arguments
codeNote.text: `na.rm = TRUE` is an optional argument: it changes how `mean()` works only when you set it. `sum()` and `max()` accept it too.

questions.ask: Partner's average is 23.2. Which line?
questions.hint: How many scores are there?
questions.ok: There are 4 scores, not 5. Dividing by length(scores) avoids counting by hand.

fb.c: print() shows what avg holds.

questions.label: Your lab partner's spreadsheet average is 23.2; R's mean is 29.

science.title: Spreadsheet header rows
science.text: A common cause of an off-by-one average is a header or blank row counted as data. Recount the values, not the rows.

codeNote.title: Counting with code, not by hand
codeNote.text: `sum(v) / length(v)` is the same as `mean(v)` and stays right when items are added or removed. A typed count like 5 goes stale.

pics.text: My spreadsheet average for this read is 23.2.

lessons.title: Write avg_quality()
lessons.intro: Please wrap the quality check in a function, so you can reuse it on every read.
lessons.doneSub: One function now checks any read at any cutoff.

questions.ask: What does the new function return?
questions.hint: Whatever goes in the brackets of the call becomes s.
questions.ok: Inside the function, s holds c(40, 30, 20), and return() hands back its mean: 30.

fb.b: That is the sum.
fb.c: That is the count.

questions.bridge: add a pass mark to the function.
questions.label: Three scores going into the avg_quality function; what comes out is unknown.

science.title: Why functions?
science.text: A sequencing run gives thousands of reads. A function applies the same check to every one, the same way each time.

codeNote.title: Writing a function
codeNote.text: `f = function(x) { ... }` makes a function named `f`. When you call `f(5)`, `x` holds 5 inside the braces, and `return()` hands back the result.

questions.ask: Give the pass mark a default value
questions.hint: The mean of 40, 30 and 20 is 30.
questions.ok: With cutoff = 30, mean 30 >= 30 is TRUE.

fb.b: With cutoff = 35, 30 >= 35 is FALSE.
fb.c: With cutoff = 40, 30 >= 40 is FALSE.
fb.d: With cutoff = 50, 30 >= 50 is FALSE.

questions.label: The passes function with its cutoff dial still blank.

science.title: Q30 as a default
science.text: Q30 is a common pass mark, so it makes a sensible default. Stricter projects, like clinical ones, may raise it.

codeNote.title: Default values
codeNote.text: `function(x, n = 2)` gives `n` a default. A call that leaves `n` out uses 2; a call like `f(x, n = 5)` overrides it.

questions.ask: What happens with a stricter cutoff?
questions.hint: A named argument replaces the default.
questions.ok: Naming cutoff = 35 overrides the default: 30 >= 35 is FALSE.

fb.b: TRUE was the result with the default, 30.
fb.c: The function returns a comparison, not the cutoff.

questions.bridge: your TA reviews a classmate's version.
questions.label: The same read through passes with the cutoff raised to 35.

science.title: Stricter cutoffs
science.text: Raising the cutoff keeps fewer reads but more reliable ones. Choosing it is a trade-off between data volume and error rate.

codeNote.title: Naming arguments in a call
codeNote.text: `f(x, cutoff = 35)` sets `cutoff` by name, so it does not matter where it sits in the brackets. Unnamed values fill the arguments in order.

questions.ask: Your TA flags this version. Which line?
questions.hint: Compare the name in function( ) with the name used inside.
questions.ok: Inside the function the input is called s, so mean(x) looks for an x that does not exist.

fb.a: Naming the input s is fine.
fb.c: The brace closes the function.
fb.d: The call is fine; the function body is wrong.

questions.bridge: check a whole read with your function.
questions.label: Your TA reviews a version that stops with: object 'x' not found.

science.title: Code review
science.text: Labs that review each other's analysis code catch errors like this before results reach a paper.

codeNote.title: Argument names inside a function
codeNote.text: The names in `function(...)` are the only inputs the function knows. Using a different name inside, like `x` instead of `s`, makes R look for it elsewhere and stop.

pics.text: This version stops with: object 'x' not found. Can you spot why?

questions.ask: Check read 1 at a cutoff of 25
questions.hint: Call passes() with the scores and cutoff = 25, inside print().
questions.ok: The mean of scores is 29, and 29 >= 25 is TRUE.
questions.label: Read 1, ready to go through your passes function.

science.title: Reusing a check
science.text: The same function now works on any read and any cutoff, which is how pipelines process thousands of reads.

codeNote.title: Calling your own function
codeNote.text: Your function works like a built-in one: `passes(scores, cutoff = 25)` sends the scores in and gets one `TRUE` or `FALSE` back.

questions.wrongBuild: The line is print(passes(scores, cutoff = 25)): passes() returns TRUE or FALSE and print() shows it.

lessons.title: Check a second read

lessons.doneSub: Read 1 is better, and read 2 fails at Q30 after the fix.

questions.ask: What is read 2's mean quality?

fb.b: That is the sum.

science.title: Replicate reads
science.text: Sequencing the same sample twice shows how consistent the run was. Big differences between reads point to a problem with one of them.

codeNote.title: Two vectors side by side
codeNote.text: You can keep several vectors at once, like `a = c(1, 2)` and `b = c(5, 6)`, and use each by name. `mean(b)` only looks at `b`.

questions.ask: Is read 1 better than read 2?
questions.hint: Read 1's mean is 29.
questions.ok: 29 > 21.5 is TRUE: read 1 is better on average.

fb.b: FALSE: 29 is not less than 21.5.
fb.c: FALSE: the means differ.
fb.d: A single = is not a comparison; R stops with an error.

questions.bridge: put both means side by side.
questions.label: The mean of read 1, 29, against read 2, 21.5.

science.title: Picking the better read
science.text: When reads disagree, the higher-quality one is usually trusted for base calls, and the other is flagged for a closer look.

codeNote.title: Comparing two results
codeNote.text: `mean(a) > mean(b)` works out both means first, then compares them, giving one `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

questions.ask: How does R print both means together?
questions.hint: c() keeps the two values side by side.
questions.ok: R prints the numbers in a vector with the same number of decimals: 29.0 and 21.5.

fb.b: R pads 29 to 29.0 to match 21.5.
fb.c: That adds the two means; c() keeps them separate.

questions.bridge: find the best read in code.
questions.label: Both read means, about to be printed side by side.

science.title: Reporting replicates
science.text: Showing both values, not only the better one, lets a reader judge how much the reads agree.

codeNote.title: Printing a vector of decimals
codeNote.text: When R prints several numbers together it gives them all the same number of decimal places, so `c(2, 1.5)` prints as 2.0 1.5.

questions.ask: Find the position of the best read
questions.hint: You want the position, not the value.
questions.ok: which.max() returns the position of the largest value: read 1.
questions.bridge: your collaborator's script needs a look.
questions.label: The two means; which position holds the larger one is unknown.

science.title: Automating the choice
science.text: With hundreds of replicates, code that picks the best one by position avoids copying numbers by hand.

codeNote.title: Positions of extremes
codeNote.text: `max(v)` gives the largest value; `which.max(v)` gives its position. `which.min()` does the same for the smallest.

questions.wrongBuild: The line is print(which.max(means)): which.max() gives the position of the biggest value, not the value.

questions.ask: Collaborator's script says read 2 passes. Which line?
questions.hint: Is the cutoff argument ever used?
questions.ok: The function ignores cutoff and always compares with 20. It should use mean(s) >= cutoff.

fb.c: The brace closes the function.
fb.d: The call is fine; the function body is wrong.

questions.label: The collaborator says read 2 passes, though its mean is only 21.5.

science.title: Hard-coded thresholds
science.text: A threshold buried inside code is often missed in review. Passing it as an argument makes the rule visible in every call.

codeNote.title: Using every argument
codeNote.text: An argument only matters if the body uses it. A number typed inside the function, like 20, overrides whatever cutoff the caller sends.

lessons.title: Too big for a well?
lessons.intro: A well on this plate holds at most 200 µL. Check every volume before you pipette.
lessons.doneSub: 250 µL is too big, so the plan splits it across 2 wells.

questions.ask: Does 250 µL fit in a 200 µL well?
questions.hint: Is 250 more than 200?
questions.ok: 250 > 200 is TRUE, so the code inside { } runs.

fb.b: The condition is TRUE here, so the inside runs.
fb.c: if() uses TRUE or FALSE to decide; it does not print it.

questions.bridge: test a volume right at the limit.
questions.label: A 250 µL sample next to a well that holds 200 µL.

science.title: Overfilled wells
science.text: An overfilled well spills into its neighbours and mixes samples, which ruins both. The volume check comes before any pipetting.

codeNote.title: Running code only sometimes: `if`
codeNote.text: `if (condition) { ... }` runs the code in braces only when the condition is `TRUE`. When it is `FALSE`, R skips the braces.

questions.ask: Test a volume right at the limit
questions.hint: The limit itself is allowed.
questions.ok: 200 <= 200 is TRUE: "less than or equal" includes the limit itself.

fb.b: 200 < 200 is FALSE, so nothing prints.
fb.c: 200 > 200 is FALSE, so nothing prints.
fb.d: A single = is not a comparison; R stops with an error.

questions.label: A 200 µL sample, exactly at the limit.

science.title: Working volumes
science.text: A well's maximum is a hard limit, but most labs stay a little under it to leave room for mixing.

codeNote.title: Including the limit
codeNote.text: `<` and `>` leave the limit out; `<=` and `>=` include it. `5 < 5` is FALSE, but `5 <= 5` is TRUE.

questions.ask: Is 250 µL inside the safe range?
questions.hint: && means "and": both must be TRUE.
questions.ok: && needs both sides TRUE: 250 >= 10 is TRUE, but 250 <= 200 is FALSE.

fb.b: Only the first check passes.
fb.c: ok stores TRUE or FALSE, not text.

questions.bridge: a typo in the limit slips through.
questions.label: The safe range is 10 to 200 µL; the 250 µL sample sits above it.

science.title: Minimum volumes
science.text: Below about 10 µL, pipetting errors become a large share of the volume, so tiny volumes are as risky as overfilled ones.

codeNote.title: Two conditions with `&&`
codeNote.text: `a && b` is `TRUE` only when both `a` and `b` are `TRUE`. `a || b` is `TRUE` when at least one is.

questions.ask: The manual says 200 µL, yet 250 fits. Which line?
questions.hint: Compare the number in the condition with the manual.
questions.ok: The limit was typed as 2000, not 200, so 250 passes.

fb.c: print() only runs because the limit is wrong.
fb.d: The brace closes the if.

questions.bridge: plan what to do with 250 µL.
questions.label: The plate script says 250 µL fits, but the manual allows 200 µL.

science.title: Why one zero matters
science.text: A tenfold error in a volume limit means every check after it passes, so mistakes reach the plate unnoticed.

codeNote.title: Checking numbers in conditions
codeNote.text: A condition is only as good as its numbers. Keeping a limit in one named value, like `max_vol = 200`, means it is typed once.

pics.text: A well holds at most 200 µL.

questions.after: After the fix: nothing prints for 250

questions.ask: Plan what to do with 250 µL
questions.hint: ! means "not".
questions.ok: !ok flips FALSE to TRUE, so the message prints.
questions.label: 250 µL split across two wells of 125 µL each.

science.title: Splitting a sample
science.text: Splitting an oversized sample across two wells keeps each within its limit; the plate map records both wells.

codeNote.title: Flipping a condition with `!`
codeNote.text: `!` turns `TRUE` into `FALSE` and back: `!(3 > 5)` is `TRUE`. Use it to act when a check fails.

questions.wrongBuild: The line is if (!ok) print("split into 2 wells"): ! turns FALSE into TRUE.

lessons.title: Big or small sample
lessons.intro: Three samples: 3 million, 0.5 million and 2.5 million cells per mL. Dilute anything at 1 million or more.
lessons.doneSub: Each sample has a plan, a dilution factor and enough wells.

questions.ask: What happens to the 3 million cell sample?
questions.hint: 3e6 means 3 × 10^6.
questions.ok: 3e6 is 3 million, more than 1 million, so only the if branch runs.

fb.b: That is the else branch, for the other case.
fb.c: if and else never both run.

questions.bridge: plan all three samples at once.
questions.label: The clinic sheet with three cell counts; the plan for the first is unknown.

science.title: Why dilute dense samples
science.text: Too many cells on a plate grow into a lawn you cannot count. Diluting first gives separate colonies.

codeNote.title: Choosing between two paths: `else`
codeNote.text: `if (cond) { A } else { B }` runs A when the condition is `TRUE` and B when it is `FALSE`. Exactly one of them runs.

questions.ask: Plan all three samples at once
questions.hint: You need one choice for each of the three counts.
questions.ok: ifelse() checks every count and picks "dilute" or "plate" for each.

fb.b: if() handles one TRUE or FALSE, so R stops with an error for three.
fb.c: c() joins everything into one vector instead of choosing.
fb.d: paste() glues the pieces together instead of choosing.

questions.bridge: work out the dilution factor for sample 3.
questions.label: All three samples from the sheet, each with a plan still to choose.

science.title: Batch planning
science.text: Clinics send samples in batches. Planning every sample in one line avoids handling each tube differently by mistake.

codeNote.title: One choice per item: `ifelse()`
codeNote.text: `ifelse(test, yes, no)` checks every item of `test` and returns `yes` or `no` for each. `if()` only handles a single `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

questions.ask: How much should sample 3 be diluted?
questions.hint: ceiling() always rounds up.
questions.ok: 2.5e6 / 1e6 is 2.5, and ceiling() rounds up to 3.

fb.b: That is before rounding up.
fb.c: That rounds down; ceiling() rounds up.

questions.bridge: the sheet lists a count of exactly 1 million.
questions.label: Sample 3 has 2.5 million cells per mL; the dilution factor is unknown.

science.title: Why round up?
science.text: Rounding a dilution factor down leaves the sample slightly too dense. Rounding up errs on the side of countable plates.

codeNote.title: Rounding up and down
codeNote.text: `ceiling(2.1)` is 3 and `floor(2.9)` is 2. `round(2.5)` goes to the nearest even number, 2, so pick the function that matches your rule.

questions.ask: Exactly 1 million should be diluted. Which line?
questions.hint: Does "or more" include the limit?
questions.ok: > leaves out exactly 1 million. The protocol says "or more", so it needs >=.

fb.c: This line would be right if it ran.
fb.d: else is placed correctly.
fb.e: This line runs only because the condition is wrong.

questions.label: A sample of exactly 1 million cells is sent to plate directly.

science.title: Following the protocol wording
science.text: Protocols say "more than" or "at least" deliberately. Matching the code to the exact wording keeps results comparable between labs.

codeNote.title: Edge cases
codeNote.text: Test a condition with a value exactly on the limit. `>` and `>=` only differ there, which is where bugs hide.

questions.ask: How many 200 µL wells for the diluted sample?
questions.hint: A part-filled well still needs a whole well.
questions.ok: 150 µL × 3 = 450 µL, and 450 / 200 = 2.25, which rounds up to 3 wells.
questions.label: 450 µL of diluted sample across 200 µL wells.

science.title: Plate maps
science.text: Knowing how many wells each sample needs before you start lets you draw the plate map and avoid running out of space.

codeNote.title: Whole numbers of things
codeNote.text: When you need whole items, like wells or tubes, divide and round up with `ceiling()`, so nothing is left over.

lessons.title: Fix the else line
lessons.intro: Anyone free to look at my pH check? My if/else won't run at all.
lessons.doneSub: Three-way decisions, a vector check, and a fixed else.

questions.ask: What does R print for pH 7.4?
questions.hint: R stops at the first TRUE condition.
questions.ok: 7.4 < 7 is FALSE and 7.4 > 7 is TRUE, so R prints "basic" and skips the rest.

fb.b: neutral only runs when both checks are FALSE.
fb.c: Only one branch of an if / else if / else chain runs.

questions.label: A pH scale from 0 to 14 with the culture marked at 7.4.

science.title: pH in the lab
science.text: Most cell cultures are kept near pH 7.4, slightly basic, like blood. A medium drifting acidic often means cells are overgrowing.

codeNote.title: Three paths: `else if`
codeNote.text: `if (a) {...} else if (b) {...} else {...}` checks `a`, then `b`, and runs the first branch whose condition is `TRUE`.

questions.ask: Add the second check for pH 7
questions.hint: You need a second condition between if and else.
questions.ok: else if adds a second check: 7 < 7 and 7 > 7 are both FALSE, so the final else prints "neutral".

fb.b: A new if right after } is a syntax error; it must be else if.
fb.c: else takes no condition; with (ph > 7) after it, R stops with an error.
fb.d: while starts a loop, not a second check; R stops with an error.

questions.label: The pH scale with the culture marked exactly at 7.

science.title: Neutral pH
science.text: Pure water at 25 °C is pH 7. Buffers hold a medium near a target pH so small additions of acid or base do not swing it.

codeNote.title: Adding a second check
codeNote.text: `else if (condition)` goes between the first `if` and the final `else`. You can chain as many as you need; R still runs only one branch.

questions.ask: Check three cultures at once
questions.hint: ifelse() works through the vector item by item.
questions.ok: ifelse() checks each pH: 6.2 acid, 7.9 base, 6.8 acid.

fb.b: ifelse() gives one answer per item, not one in total.
fb.c: That error comes from if(), not ifelse(); ifelse() handles vectors.

questions.label: Three cultures marked on the pH scale at 6.2, 7.9 and 6.8.

science.title: Checking many cultures
science.text: An incubator can hold dozens of flasks. A vector check flags the ones drifting acidic in one line.

codeNote.title: `if` versus `ifelse()`
codeNote.text: `if` takes one `TRUE` or `FALSE` and runs a block of code. `ifelse()` takes a whole vector and returns one value per item.

questions.ask: A classmate's if/else won't run. Which line?
questions.hint: Where does R think the if statement ends?
questions.ok: R ends the if at the } on line 3, so else on a new line has nothing to attach to. Put it on the same line: } else {.

fb.b: This line is fine.
fb.c: The brace is fine, but R stops reading the if here.

questions.label: A classmate's if/else stops with: unexpected 'else'.

science.title: Debugging together
science.text: Explaining an error to a classmate is one of the quickest ways to understand it yourself, which is why labs share code in group chats.

codeNote.title: Where `else` goes
codeNote.text: At the top level of a script, R ends an `if` at its closing `}`. Writing `} else {` on one line tells R the `else` belongs to that `if`.

questions.ask: Label the 7.9 culture in one line
questions.hint: Store the result of the if / else in label.
questions.ok: An if / else can give back a value: 7.9 > 7, so label is "basic".
questions.label: The 7.9 culture, about to get a one-word label.

science.title: Labelling cultures
science.text: Short labels like "basic" go straight onto a plate map or into a table, ready for the next step of the protocol.

codeNote.title: `if` as a value
codeNote.text: `x = if (cond) "a" else "b"` stores whichever value is chosen. On one line, `else` sits right after the first value, so R keeps them together.

questions.wrongBuild: The line is label = if (ph > 7) "basic" else "not basic": the chosen value is stored in label.

lessons.title: Buffer to add
lessons.intro: Stock concentration 10x. Make 50 µL at 2x. All volumes in µL.
lessons.doneSub: 10 µL stock plus 40 µL buffer makes 50 µL at 2x.

questions.ask: How much stock do you need?
questions.hint: Multiply target by final, then divide by stock.
questions.ok: C1 × V1 = C2 × V2, so V1 = 2 × 50 / 10 = 10 µL of stock.

fb.c: 40 is the buffer, the rest of the volume.

questions.label: A 10x stock to be diluted to 2x in 50 µL; the stock volume is unknown.

science.title: C1V1 = C2V2
science.text: Diluting a stock keeps the amount of substance the same: concentration times volume before equals concentration times volume after.

codeNote.title: Formulas from the lab
codeNote.text: Write a lab formula with named values: `v1 = c2 * v2 / c1` reads like C1V1 = C2V2 rearranged, and can be checked line by line against the protocol.

science.title: Topping up with buffer
science.text: The buffer brings the mix to its final volume and keeps pH and salt where the experiment needs them.

codeNote.title: Building on earlier results
codeNote.text: `buffer = final - sample` uses values you already stored, so if `sample` changes, `buffer` follows when you rerun the script.

science.title: Pipetting limits
science.text: Most lab pipettes are unreliable below about 1 µL. Below that, labs make an intermediate dilution first.

codeNote.title: Guarding a calculation
codeNote.text: An `if` before an action can stop impossible steps: here, volumes too small for a pipette. The `else` carries on as normal.

science.title: Unit mix-ups
science.text: Mixing mL and µL is a thousandfold error. It is one of the most common causes of failed dilutions.

codeNote.title: Keeping units consistent
codeNote.text: R does not know units; `0.05` and `50` are only numbers. Keep every value in one unit, and say which in the name, like `final_ul`.

questions.ask: Check the parts add up
questions.hint: The parts should add up to the final volume.

science.title: Checking the total
science.text: A recipe whose parts do not add up to the final volume gives the wrong concentration, however carefully you pipette.

codeNote.title: Adding up a vector
codeNote.text: `sum(v)` adds every item of `v`. Checking that parts add up to the whole is a quick test of any recipe.
